hero.name: Paweł Szeliga
hero.tagline: I build fast, well-structured applications — from React interfaces down to the .NET and Python backends behind them — and I like figuring out how the pieces fit together.
hero.location: Warsaw, Poland — open to junior / graduate developer roles

about.title: A developer who ships, not just studies
about.p1: I'm a Computer Science graduate who recently spent six months as a software intern at Veolia CUW, building automations, scraping modules and a full-stack app for real client-facing projects — not classroom exercises. That, plus 12+ personal and academic builds, is where most of what I know actually came from.
about.p2: I move comfortably between the frontend and backend: React and TypeScript on one side, C#/.NET, Python and Java on the other, with relational databases underneath. I care about code that the next person — often future me — can actually read.

experience.title: Where I've put it to work

items.description: Built process automations, web-scraping modules and an operational app in AppSheet, and shipped a full-stack application — all on the team's real client-facing projects, not sandboxed exercises. First taste of production code, code review, and deadlines that affect actual users.
Set up and operated live AV systems for conferences, troubleshooting hardware and software issues in real time under a hard deadline — no room for “it works on my machine.”

Designed and shipped 12+ projects spanning full-stack web apps, a REST API in ASP.NET Core, a machine-learning image classifier, and a neural network built from scratch. Worked in small teams using Git, task tracking, and code review.

skills.title: Tools I reach for
skills.tapHint: Tap a skill for a plain-English explanation

descriptions.typescript: A version of JavaScript that adds safety checks before an app even runs, catching typos and mistakes early. It's what most modern web interfaces — including this site — are built with.
descriptions.javascript: The core programming language that makes websites interactive — the thing that responds when you click a button or scroll the page. It runs in every web browser.
descriptions.python: A widely-used, readable programming language popular for automation, data analysis and machine learning. I use it for scripting, AI/ML projects and backend work.
descriptions.java: A mature, widely-used programming language known for building reliable, large-scale applications. Common in enterprise software and Android apps.
descriptions.csharp: Microsoft's programming language for building backend systems and enterprise applications. I use it together with the .NET framework.
descriptions.cpp: A fast, low-level programming language used when performance really matters — games, simulations, systems software.
descriptions.sql: The standard language for asking questions of a database — 'find me all customers from Warsaw,' for example. Nearly every app with stored data uses it somewhere.
descriptions.react: A popular toolkit (by Meta/Facebook) for building the parts of a website you see and interact with, out of reusable, snap-together pieces.
descriptions.html5: The basic building blocks of every web page — the structure and content, like headings, paragraphs and images. It's the skeleton every website is built on.
descriptions.css3: The styling language that makes web pages look good — colors, spacing, layout, animations. If HTML is the skeleton, this is the skin and clothes.
descriptions.tailwindcss: A modern toolkit for styling websites quickly and consistently, without writing custom styling code from scratch for every element.
descriptions.framermotion: A library for adding smooth animations and transitions to a website — the sliding, fading and moving effects you see as you scroll this page.
descriptions.figma: A design tool for planning what an app or website should look like before it's built — like a blueprint, but interactive.
descriptions.aspnetcore: Microsoft's framework for building the 'server side' of an application — the part that handles logins, processes data and talks to a database, invisible to the end user.
descriptions.nodejsexpress: A way of running JavaScript on the server instead of just in the browser, used to build the backend of an app — the part that stores and serves data.
descriptions.restapis: A standard way for two pieces of software to talk to each other — for example, how a mobile app asks a server for your account information.
descriptions.postgresql: A free, powerful database system used to store an application's data reliably — user accounts, orders, messages, anything that needs to be saved and looked up later.
descriptions.mssqlserver: Microsoft's database system, commonly used in businesses to store and manage large amounts of data securely.
descriptions.redis: An extremely fast, temporary storage system used to speed up applications — for example, remembering a logged-in user so the app doesn't have to check the database on every click.
descriptions.databasedesign: Planning how an application's information should be organized and connected — customers, orders, products — so it stays fast, accurate and easy to work with as it grows.
descriptions.appsheet: A no-code tool by Google for building working business apps — forms, trackers, dashboards — by configuring a spreadsheet instead of writing traditional code. Great for automating everyday business processes quickly.
descriptions.oopdesignpatterns: A way of organizing code around real-world concepts (like 'Customer' or 'Order') and proven, reusable solutions to common problems — it makes software easier to build correctly and maintain later.
descriptions.datastructuresalgorithms: The fundamental techniques for organizing information and solving problems efficiently — the difference between a program that handles a million users smoothly and one that grinds to a halt.
descriptions.osnetworks: Understanding how computers manage their resources internally, and how they communicate with each other over the internet — the plumbing beneath every app.
descriptions.discretemathlogic: The mathematical reasoning that underpins computer science — logical thinking, structured problem-solving, and the theory behind how algorithms work.
descriptions.git: A tool that tracks every change made to a project's code over time, so nothing is ever lost and multiple people can safely work on the same project together.
descriptions.docker: A tool that packages an application together with everything it needs to run, so it behaves identically on any computer — solving the classic 'it works on my machine' problem.
descriptions.unittesting: Writing small, automated checks that verify individual pieces of code work correctly — catching bugs early, before they ever reach a real user.
descriptions.technicaldocumentation: Writing clear explanations of how a system works, so other developers (or future me) can understand and maintain it without reverse-engineering everything.
descriptions.agileteamwork: A way of working in a team that breaks big projects into small, manageable chunks with regular check-ins — so progress stays visible and plans can adapt as things change.
descriptions.claude: Anthropic's AI coding assistant, which I use as a pair-programmer for planning changes, writing and reviewing code, and moving faster without giving up understanding of what's actually happening under the hood. This site itself was built working with it.
